It has been revealed that TL;DR: Ethlabs proposes quantum readiness in 2027 and aims to withdraw its quick-slots work from Hegotá. Developers still need to agree on the network's priorities.

Industry observers note that ethereum's next upgrade debate is becoming a question of how much engineering effort should move toward long-term security. In a November 11 proposal, Ethlabs argues for making quantum protection and resilience against advanced AI-assisted attacks the priority for 2027.

The practical question is which improvements can share an upgrade without slowing the security work. That trade-off deserves attention even from readers who never run a validator: protocol roadmaps influence the software that wallets, exchanges and applications must eventually support.

Recent findings suggest that ethlabs distinguishes basic readiness from full performance: keeping Ethereum operational with quantum-safe options is the main objective, while matching full network capacity is the more ambitious goal. Its proposed reshuffle includes withdrawing quick slots from Hegotá and reconsidering work outside that security objective.

This is a contribution to Ethereum's development process. A research group's preferred date does not establish an activation date, and an architectural direction still needs specifications, implementations and testing. The useful evidence from here will be what client teams agree to build and what they can demonstrate together.

NewsBTC's earlier coverage of Ethereum's proposed base-layer reconstruction helps explain why changes to speed, security and account design have become closely connected.

One relevant building block is EIP-8141, the frame-transaction proposal. It would let a transaction contain separate steps for validation, fee approval and execution. The design gives accounts more flexibility over how they authorise activity, including a path away from today's elliptic-curve signatures.

It also provides for key rotation, batched operations and alternative fee payment. Those features matter because a cryptographic migration is easier to manage when an account's identity can survive a change in its authorisation method.

That creates an key implementation question. An upgrade can enable a safer signature scheme, but wallet developers still have to expose it clearly, exchanges have to recognise it, and owners need a recovery path that they understand. Flexibility in the protocol only becomes useful protection when the surrounding software makes it usable.

Ethereum's quantum-security overview identifies multiple areas of exposure: ordinary account signatures, validator signatures, data commitments and some proof systems. Each has a different role, so replacing one component would leave other migration work outstanding.

The same overview indicates present-day quantum computers cannot break Ethereum's cryptography. Preparation is being undertaken because a transition across a large network takes time, while future hardware capability is uncertain. Hash-based approaches are among the routes being researched, with different efficiency and deployment challenges from current systems.

According to recent reports, the distinction between a future cryptographic threat and an active compromise is essential. Readers should not interpret a more ambitious research timetable as evidence that current Ethereum accounts have suddenly been broken. NewsBTC has previously examined Justin Drake's view of quantum migration as a broader redesign opportunity.

It has been revealed that our reading is that the proposal's significance lies in resource allocation. Every additional feature creates implementation and review work, while concentrating on security can defer improvements that other consumers want sooner. Neither choice is costless.

Industry observers note that A credible programme therefore needs measurable milestones: working clients, agreement on migration behaviour and evidence about performance under the new cryptography. It also needs a clear account of which guarantees are available at each stage.

According to recent reports, for ETH holders, those milestones will be more informative than a calendar target alone. The debate now asks developers to turn an ambitious security objective into a sequence that the wider Ethereum ecosystem can actually deliver.

Bitcoin fell below $70,000 as crypto sentiment hit its lowest level in more than four months, with analysts warning of institutional outflows, thinning liquidity and elevated leverage.

Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Friday, extending its recent decline as investor sentiment deteriorated amid institutional outflows, tightening liquidity and broader macroeconomic pressures.

Vikram Subburaj, CEO of crypto exchange Giottus, attributed Bitcoin’s weakness to institutional outflows, tightening crypto liquidity and expectations of a December Federal Reserve interest rate hike. “Investors should avoid chasing short-term dips or using excessive leverage,” he said.

It has been revealed that in a Friday report, 10x Research highlighted Bitcoin’s divergence from US equities. Between Nov. 5 and Nov. 12, Bitcoin declined 5.9% while the Nasdaq 100 gained 6.4%, suggesting the cryptocurrency was responding more to rising Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar than to technology stocks.

The research firm said Bitcoin was increasingly trading alongside gold, which fell 5.5% over the same period, as the US 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 5%.

Meanwhile, institutional trading platform Talos also warned that thin liquidity and elevated leverage could amplify market volatility. Its weekly report highlighted Bitcoin order-book depth across major exchanges fell to $72 million on Nov. 9, roughly 33% below normal levels.

“Liquidity remains thin while leverage stays elevated, leaving the market vulnerable to sharp moves in either direction,” noted Tanay Ved, senior research associate at Talos. “A rebuild in order-book depth and a turn in capital flows would provide a firmer foundation for recovery.”.

According to recent reports, the selloff follows sustained withdrawals from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs). BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded more than $2 billion in net outflows across nine consecutive trading sessions through Wednesday, while broader funds shed nearly $1.44 billion over five sessions.

North Korea Stole $400 Million in Crypto Using Deepfake Video Calls, DOJ Says.

According to recent reports, north Korean hackers have stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months using a social-engineering scheme built on secretly recorded footage and AI deepfakes, the U.S. Justice Department said Thursday, as it revealed the seizure of the infrastructure behind the operation.

Recent findings suggest that the scheme, which the FBI calls “FaceStealer,” turns video conference calls into a trap. According to the DOJ, hackers lure targets into meetings using accounts stolen from previous victims, then play prerecorded webcam footage of trusted contacts to simulate their presence and win the target’s confidence.

The group also generates deepfake videos of well-known figures in the crypto and related industries, using AI to make the ruse more convincing.

Once a target is at ease, the attackers manufacture a fake technical glitch, such as claiming the person can’t be heard, and offer a link to “fix” it, which instead installs malware.

From there, the hackers can drain crypto wallets or exploit the victim’s access to other systems, sometimes waiting months or more than a year before striking. The FBI said it seized over 900 webcam recordings of FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant.

The DOJ tied the operation to North Korean groups known variously as Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff and APT38, among others, and warned the hackers have increasingly targeted open-source software developers in an apparent bid to enable supply-chain attacks.

Recent findings suggest that the announcement came paired with an upgrade on the record-breaking Binance hack. The department said it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the roughly $6.4 billion stolen from the exchange on Oct. 29, part of over $2.7 billion frozen so far.

It has been revealed that the FBI attributed that theft to the North Korean group TraderTraitor, and the regime has been laundering the proceeds at speed, spinning up a newly introduced wallet roughly every 25 seconds. North Korea has denied involvement, calling the FBI’s finding a political provocation.

Sources indicate that the actions underscore how central crypto theft has become to Pyongyang’s finances. The U.S. recently sanctioned 11 people over a North Korean IT-worker scheme that moved millions in crypto, and researchers have cataloged the many ways the regime’s hackers break into crypto firms.

Officials said efforts to trace and recover the stolen Binance funds are ongoing.
